subject: Sillence et al. (1979)
object: In an epidemiologic and genetic study of osteogenesis imperfecta in Victoria, Australia, Sillence et al. (1979) concluded that there were at least four distinct syndromes then called OI. Type I showed autosomal dominant osteoporosis with fractures, distinctly blue sclerae and presenile conductive hearing loss. Type II was perinatal lethal, with broad, crumpled femora and beaded ribs, and was likely autosomal recessive in some or all cases. Type III was progressively deforming, with sclerae that became less blue with age. Type IV was dominant, with variable deformity and normal sclerae.

subject: Sillence et al. (1979)
object: Sillence et al. (1979) described a third, progressively deforming group of OI patients, two-thirds of whom had fractures at birth. They had severe progressive deformity of the limbs and spine, and their scleral blueness was less intense than in the first group and decreased with age. All were sporadic cases. The mode of inheritance was not resolved, but the authors considered it likely that the group was heterogeneous, with both dominant and recessive genotypes responsible.

subject: Munns et al. (2004)
object: Munns et al. (2004) described 3 unrelated children with an apparently novel bone fragility disorder associated with an idiopathic mineralization defect. Recurrent lower limb fractures began with weight bearing. The patients had none of the phenotypic, radiologic, or histomorphometric features classically associated with osteogenesis imperfecta, idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis, or mild autosomal dominant osteopetrosis. The authors concluded that this was a bone fragility disorder of moderate severity that tends to cause lower extremity fractures.

subject: Munns et al. (2004)
object: On radiographs, the patients described by Munns et al. (2004) had increased metaphyseal trabeculation and normal to increased cortical thickness, with no evidence of rickets or osteomalacia. Areal and volumetric bone mineral density of the lumbar spine showed no major change. In 1 patient, peripheral quantitative CT of the radius showed increased cortical thickness and increased total and trabecular volumetric bone mineral density.

subject: Munns et al. (2004)
object: In the patients described by Munns et al. (2004), qualitative histology of iliac bone biopsies showed a paucity of the birefringent pattern of normal lamellar bone. Quantitative histomorphometry showed osteomalacia, with a prolonged mineralization lag time and a decreased mineral apposition rate. The authors concluded that the disorder involves accumulation of osteoid caused by an intrinsic mineralization defect.

subject: Munns et al. (2004)
object: Munns et al. (2004) found no biochemical evidence of abnormal calcium or phosphate metabolism in the 3 patients.

subject: Munns et al. (2004)
object: Munns et al. (2004) found no type I collagen mutations in the 3 patients. They stated that the pathogenetic basis of the disorder remained to be elucidated.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) described a 15-year-old Egyptian girl (II-3), born to first-cousin parents, with severe autosomal recessive OI. A fracture of the left tibia was noted after birth, and she went on to have 10 to 15 spontaneous fractures per year. Other features were a triangular face, faint blue sclerae, no dentinogenesis imperfecta, normal mental development, a large thorax, and a large umbilical hernia containing abdominal contents. She also had hypotonia, generalized hirsutism, severe bone deformities, arachnodactyly, joint hyperextensibility, kyphoscoliosis, pectus carinatum, platyspondyly, wormian bones, severe short stature (length -11.5 SD), and borderline osteoporosis on DEXA.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) described the 5-year-old brother (II-6) of the proband. Bilateral femoral bowing was seen on prenatal ultrasound, and both femora were fractured at birth. He had about 15 fractures per year, facial features like his sister's, no dentinogenesis imperfecta, normal mentality, joint hyperextensibility, arachnodactyly, and a large umbilical hernia. Other findings were wormian bones, scoliosis, platyspondyly, and osteoporosis. In both sibs, hearing and cardiovascular examinations were unremarkable, serum calcium and phosphate were normal, and alkaline phosphatase was slightly high. Both were diagnosed with OI Sillence type III.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) carried out genome-wide homozygosity mapping in the 2 affected sibs and 2 unaffected sibs. This excluded the known AR-OI loci, and COL1A1/COL1A2 sequencing found no mutations. The analysis identified 2 homozygous regions shared only by the affected sibs: 35.4 Mb on chromosome 3 and 10.27 Mb on chromosome 8p. The 8p region contained BMP1.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: In 2 sibs with OI type III from a consanguineous Egyptian family, Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) identified a homozygous c.747C>G transversion in exon 6 of the BMP1 gene, causing a phe249-to-leu (F249L) substitution. Phe249 lies in the protease domain and is conserved in all astacin metalloproteases. Both unaffected sibs and both parents were heterozygous. The variant was absent from 100 control chromosomes of the same ethnicity and from 884 European control chromosomes.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) studied fibroblasts from the 2 patients. In both, the ratio of pN-alpha-1(I) to pC-alpha-1(I) was reduced and free PICP was decreased, showing diminished procollagen I C-propeptidase activity, although some residual activity remained. A heterozygous sib's fibroblasts showed slight impairment. Collagen was not overmodified, and BMP1/mTLD protein levels were normal.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) overexpressed wildtype and mutant mTLD in NIH3T3 cells and in human primary fibroblasts. Wildtype mTLD caused most pro-alpha-1(I) to be C-terminally processed, whereas the F249L mutant did not increase cleavage. Only the wildtype protein rescued processing in patient fibroblasts. The authors concluded that the mutation strongly reduces BMP1/mTLD proteolytic function.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) noted that Bmp1-null mice die perinatally and have no gross skeletal abnormalities at birth apart from reduced ossification of some skull bones. However, the mice consistently show herniation of the gut, a feature shared with the large umbilical hernias in the patients.

subject: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012)
object: Martínez-Glez et al. (2012) reported that both affected sibs were started on cyclic intravenous bisphosphonate injections.

subject: Asharani et al. (2012)
object: Asharani et al. (2012) studied a consanguineous family affected by increased bone mineral density and multiple recurrent fractures.

subject: Asharani et al. (2012)
object: By whole-exome sequencing combined with filtering for homozygous stretches, Asharani et al. (2012) identified a homozygous c.34G>C mutation in the BMP1 gene, located in the signal peptide, in a consanguineous family with increased bone mineral density and recurrent fractures. The mutation led to impaired secretion and an alteration in posttranslational modification.

subject: Asharani et al. (2012)
object: Asharani et al. (2012) characterized a zebrafish bone mutant harboring lesions in bmp1a, demonstrating conservation of BMP1 function in osteogenesis. Genetic, biochemical, and histologic analyses of this mutant and comparison to a second similar locus showed that Bmp1a is critically required for mature collagen generation, downstream of osteoblast maturation, in bone.

subject: Valencia et al. (2014)
object: Valencia et al. (2014) described an additional patient with osteogenesis imperfecta who had normal bone density.

subject: Valencia et al. (2014)
object: In a patient with osteogenesis imperfecta and normal bone density, Valencia et al. (2014) identified a recurrent homozygous c.34G>C mutation in the BMP1 gene. Western blot analysis of the patient's dermal fibroblasts showed decreased protein levels of both alternatively spliced BMP1 products and abnormal cleavage of the C-terminal propeptide of type I procollagen.

subject: Valencia et al. (2014)
object: Valencia et al. (2014) used fluorescence and electron microscopy to show impaired assembly of type I collagen fibrils in the extracellular matrix of cultured fibroblasts from 2 patients: their patient with the homozygous BMP1 c.34G>C mutation and a previously reported patient with a homozygous BMP1 c.747C>G mutation. They concluded that BMP1 is essential for human type I collagen fibrillogenesis.

subject: Fahiminiya et al. (2015)
object: Fahiminiya et al. (2015) studied 4 unrelated children with a bone fragility disorder that they had previously described. The disorder was characterized mainly by lower extremity fractures and by a mineralization defect in bone tissue but not at the growth plate level. Peripheral quantitative computed tomography showed elevated volumetric cortical bone mineral density in all 4 individuals.

subject: Fahiminiya et al. (2015)
object: In iliac bone samples from the patients, Fahiminiya et al. (2015) found by histomorphometry and quantitative backscattered electron imaging that the onset of mineralization at bone formation sites was delayed, but that the mineralized matrix was hypermineralized.

subject: Fahiminiya et al. (2015)
object: Using whole-exome sequencing in 4 unrelated individuals, Fahiminiya et al. (2015) found that 3 were homozygous for a variant in BMP1 (c.*241T>C) that affects the polyadenylation signal of the transcript encoding the short isoform, BMP1-1. Skin fibroblasts from these individuals had low levels of BMP1-1 transcript and protein. Less free procollagen type I C-propeptide was present in the fibroblast supernatant than in controls, which indicated impaired C-propeptide cleavage. The authors concluded that isolated lack of BMP1-1 causes bone fragility in children.

subject: Fahiminiya et al. (2015)
object: Fahiminiya et al. (2015) found that the fourth individual was compound heterozygous for the BMP1 c.*241T>C polyadenylation-signal variant in BMP1-1 and a BMP1 exon 15 variant (c.2107G>C). The exon 15 variant affected splicing of both BMP1-1 and the long isoform, BMP1-3. Patient skin fibroblasts showed impaired cleavage of the procollagen type I C-propeptide.

subject: Cho et al. (2015)
object: Cho et al. (2015) described a Korean patient with osteogenesis imperfecta who had an umbilical hernia, frequent fractures, markedly short stature, delayed motor development, scoliosis, and dislocation of the radial head with a bowed radius and ulna.

subject: Cho et al. (2015)
object: In a Korean patient with osteogenesis imperfecta, Cho et al. (2015) used whole-exome sequencing and identified compound heterozygous novel variants in the BMP1 gene. One was a c.808A>G transition resulting in a met270-to-val (M270V) substitution. The other was a c.1297G>T change that caused skipping of exon 10. A zebrafish assay showed that both variants were hypofunctional.

subject: Cho et al. (2015)
object: Cho et al. (2015) tested the BMP1 variants c.808A>G (p.Met270Val) and c.1297G>T (exon 10 skipping) in a zebrafish assay and showed that both were hypofunctional.
